title: 〜ことで (means)
meaning: Shows that doing something leads to a result or change: “by doing ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form / ない-form / た-form + ことで

senses.label: Means / method
senses.meaning: Presents an action as the means, and the second clause gives the effect. Like “by (doing) ...”. The second clause is usually a change, an effect, or an ability. A bit more conversational than 「〜によって」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form / ない-form + ことで (second clause often 「〜ようになる」, 「〜できる」, 「〜られる」)
examples: By exercising every day, I got stronger.
By keeping a diary in Japanese, I improved my writing.
I keep my calories down by not using sugar.

senses.label: Cause / trigger
senses.meaning: With the た-form, something that has already happened becomes the trigger for what follows. Like “because ...” or “now that ...”. The second clause is a change that has already taken place.
senses.connection: Verb た-form + ことで (second clause usually a past result)
examples: The town got livelier because a new station was built.
With just one apology from him, the two of them were back on good terms.

notes: 「〜ことで」 expresses “means → effect,” not purpose. To say “do X in order to ...” use 「ために」: ✕「合格することで、毎日勉強している」→ ○「合格するために、毎日勉強している」; ○「毎日勉強することで、合格できた」. Swapping the two clauses changes the meaning completely.
You can't attach 「ことで」 directly to a noun: ✕「バスことで行く」→ ○「バスで行く」／「バスを使うことで、時間を節約する」. What comes before 「ことで」 must be a verb (clause).
The 「で」 in 「このことで」 and 「そのことで」 means “about”: 「そのことで相談があります」 means “I'd like to talk to you about that,” not “by means of that.”
「〜ことで有名だ」 and 「〜ことで知られる」 mean “famous for ...,” not means: 「この町は温泉があることで有名だ」.

daily.title: Sharing a study tip
daily.description: Telling a friend your trick for improving your Japanese.
daily.example: Reading aloud will improve your pronunciation.

daily.title: Talking about healthy habits
daily.description: Chatting with family about how you get a little more exercise.
daily.example: I try to get a bit of exercise by not taking the elevator.

work.title: Proposing an improvement
work.description: Explaining the effect of a new plan to your boss in a meeting.
work.example: By automating the work, we can cut costs by 30%.

work.title: News on policy results
work.description: A news report explains what a change in the system brought about.
work.example: Thanks to the review of the system, the number of children on daycare waiting lists has dropped sharply.

etymology: The formal noun 「こと」 turns the preceding action into a noun. Then the particle 「で」, which marks means or cause, is added. Literally: “with the fact of doing ... as the means (or cause)”.

similar.title: 〜で (means / method)
similar.explanation: Same origin, close in meaning: 「で」 attaches directly to a noun to show a tool or means (「電車で行く」); 「ことで」 first turns the action into a noun with 「こと」 and then adds the same 「で」, so a whole way of doing something can serve as the means (「電車を使うことで時間を節約する」).

similar.title: 〜によって
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「〜ことによって」 and 「〜ことにより」 mean basically the same as 「〜ことで」, but are more formal and appear mostly in papers, news, and official documents. 「によって」 can also attach directly to a noun (「話し合いによって解決する」).

similar.title: 〜ことから
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both are built on 「こと」 and can express a cause. 「ことから」 focuses on the grounds for a judgment or the origin of a name (“from this you can tell / hence the name”); 「ことで」 focuses on the effect or change that an action or event brings about.

formation: 「〜ことで」 = the formal noun 「こと」 + the case particle 「で」. 「こと」 turns the verb clause before it into a “noun” (one thing), so it can take a case particle. 「で」 already marks means (「ペンで書く」) and cause (「病気で休む」), so 「運動することで」 means “by means of the act of exercising.” After the dictionary form or ない-form the focus is on method, so the means reading is stronger; after the た-form it describes something that has already happened, so the cause/trigger reading is stronger. Because 「で」 marks “what you rely on,” the second clause naturally gives the effect or change that results, which is why 「〜ようになる」 and 「〜できる」 often follow.

title: 〜たものだ (reminiscing)
meaning: Looks back fondly on things you used to do often, or on how things used to be: “I used to ...”.
connection: Verb た-form + ものだ (casual: 〜たもんだ)

senses.label: Reminiscing
senses.meaning: Recalls something that happened again and again in the past, with a nostalgic, sentimental tone. Like “back then, I would often ...”. Often used with 「よく」, 「昔は」, or 「〜ころは」.
senses.connection: Verb た-form + ものだ／ものです／ものだった
examples: When I was a child, I often swam in this river.
In my student days, I used to talk with friends until morning.
This area used to be quiet, too.

senses.label: Marveling at change
senses.meaning: Expresses surprise or deep feeling about a change that has happened. Like “my, how ... has ...!”. Often used with 「ずいぶん」 or 「よく」.
senses.connection: Verb た-form + ものだ (common: 大きくなったものだ, 変わったものだ)
examples: My daughter was so small, and look how she's grown!
This town has really changed, hasn't it?

notes: Use it only for things that happened repeatedly and habitually in the past; a one-time experience won't work: ✕「去年、京都へ行ったものだ」→ ○「去年、京都へ行った」／「京都へ行ったことがある」.
You can only look back on habits that have ended; something still going on can't use it: ✕「今でも毎朝走ったものだ」→ ○「今でも毎朝走っている」.

Don't confuse it with 「〜たものではない」: that one attaches to the potential form and means “there's no way to ...” (「この料理は食べられたものではない」 = “this dish is so bad it can't be eaten”), and has nothing to do with nostalgia.
「母が作ったものだ」 may also simply mean “this is something my mother made” (a real noun); judge by the context and by words like 「よく」 or 「昔は」.

daily.title: Talking about childhood
daily.description: Friends reminisce about growing up.
daily.example: In elementary school, I'd play outside every day until it got dark.

daily.title: Class reunion
daily.description: Old classmates get together and recall their school days.
daily.example: We used to get scolded by the teacher in class all the time, didn't we?

daily.title: Visiting your hometown
daily.description: Back home after a long time, you're struck by how it's changed.
daily.example: The area in front of the station has gotten so lively.

work.title: A veteran on the old days
work.description: A long-time employee tells a newcomer what work was like when they were young.
work.example: When I was new, I used to work late every night.

work.title: Reading an essay
work.description: In essays and memoirs, writers look back on the past.
work.example: In the Showa era, every home had a black telephone.

etymology: Made of the formal noun 「もの」 plus 「だ」. 「もの」 sums up past events as “the way things were back then”, which gives the expression its nostalgic, sentimental tone.

similar.title: 〜ものだ (common sense / feeling)
similar.explanation: Same origin: also 「もの＋だ」. With the dictionary form it states the nature of things, a general truth (「子供はよく遊ぶものだ」 = kids just love to play); with the た-form it is reminiscing (「よく遊んだものだ」 = I used to play a lot). A different tense means a different meaning.

similar.title: 〜たことがある
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both talk about the past. 「たことがある」 just states objectively that you have had an experience, even once, with no feeling attached; 「たものだ」 must be about something that happened repeatedly at the time, and carries nostalgia.

similar.title: 〜ている
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「よく〜ていた」 can also express a past habit (「昔はよくこの川で泳いでいた」), but only as a plain statement; 「〜たものだ」 adds the speaker's nostalgia and sentiment.

formation: 「〜たものだ」 = the た-form (past) + the formal noun 「もの」 + 「だ」. 「もの」 doesn't point to a specific thing but to “a general state of affairs, the way things were,” so the construction sums up a past action as “that's how it used to be”: 「よく泳いだものだ」 = “I used to swim here a lot, that's how it was back then.” Looking back on a stretch of the past as one habitual whole naturally brings out nostalgia, and precisely because it describes a “normal pattern,” it works only for repeated habits, not one-off events. With verbs of change such as 「大きくなった」 or 「変わった」, the result of the change is treated as something worth marveling at, which gives the feeling of amazement.

title: 〜ものだ (common sense / feeling)
meaning: States the nature of things or social common sense (“that's just how it is”). Also used to give advice, or to exclaim about something (“how ...!”).
connection: Verb dictionary form / ない-form, い-adjective + ものだ; な-adjective + な + ものだ

senses.label: Nature / common sense
senses.meaning: Describes the general nature of things or of people. Like “... naturally ...” or “that's how it is”. It's about general rules, not individual cases.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form / ない-form + ものだ
examples: Everyone makes mistakes.
Parents always worry about their children.
The better the medicine, the more bitter it tastes.

senses.label: Advice / should
senses.meaning: Uses social common sense to tell someone what they “should” do. Softer than 「〜べきだ」. The negative is 「〜ものではない」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ものだ (often from older to younger people)
examples: You should hear people out until they finish.
You should use keigo with people above you.

senses.label: Exclamation
senses.meaning: Expresses wonder about something in front of you. Like “how ...!” or “... really is ...”. Often used with 「本当に」, 「なあ」, or 「ね」.
senses.connection: い-adjective / な-adjective + な + ものだ
examples: Time really flies, doesn't it?
Life is a strange thing.

notes: The advice use appeals to “social common sense” to instruct the listener. Saying 「〜するものですよ」 to a superior or a customer implies they don't know common sense, which is very rude; use it only to juniors and children.

With the dictionary form it is a general truth, and with the た-form it turns into reminiscing, so getting the tense wrong changes the meaning: 「子供はよく遊ぶものだ」 (children just love to play) ↔ 「子供のころはよく遊んだものだ」 (I played a lot as a kid).
The negative of the advice use is 「〜ものではない」 (“you shouldn't ...”): 「人の悪口を言うものではない」. Don't say ✕「〜ものではないだ」 or ✕「〜ものじゃないだ」.
It expresses a general rule, not a specific individual fact: ✕「田中さんは毎日遅刻するものだ」 (it sounds like a verdict, “that's just the kind of person Tanaka is”) → ○「田中さんは毎日遅刻する」.

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: Your friend is down after failing, so you tell them it happens to everyone.
daily.example: Everyone fails sometimes, you know.

daily.title: End-of-year reflection
daily.description: At the end of the year, you and your family marvel at how fast it went.
daily.example: A year really goes by in a flash, doesn't it?

daily.title: Parents teaching kids
daily.description: Parents teach their children basic manners.
daily.example: You wash your hands before you eat.

work.title: A senior coaching a newcomer
work.description: A senior employee explains workplace common sense to a new hire.
work.example: You should answer the phone as quickly as you can.

work.title: Reading an opinion piece
work.description: In an essay, the writer reflects on life.
work.example: You only realize how precious good health is once you've lost it.

etymology: 「もの」 originally means “thing”, extended to “the general nature of things”. Adding 「だ」 gives “that's just how things are”, which developed into the advice and exclamation uses.

similar.title: 〜べきだ
similar.explanation: Close in meaning (advice): 「べきだ」 is the speaker's own strong assertion or judgment of duty, and sounds hard; 「ものだ」 persuades by appealing to “common sense,” which is softer but still sounds preachy.

similar.title: 〜ことだ (advice)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning (advice): 「ことだ」 gives a specific suggestion to the person in front of you (「よく休むことだ」); 「ものだ」 states a general principle that applies to everyone.

similar.title: 〜というものだ
similar.explanation: Same origin, close in meaning: both use 「もの」 to talk about the essence of things. 「というものだ」 is mostly used to pass judgment on a specific matter (「それはわがままというものだ」 = that's what you call selfishness); 「ものだ」 states a general nature or common sense.

similar.title: 〜たものだ (reminiscing)
similar.explanation: Same origin: attaches to the た-form, and expresses nostalgia for things one often did, or amazement at change (「ずいぶん変わったものだ」).

formation: 「〜ものだ」 = the formal noun 「もの」 + the copula 「だ」. 「もの」 originally means “thing,” but here it doesn't point to one item; it refers to “this kind of thing as a whole,” so 「〜ものだ」 means “that's just what such things are like.” It files an individual case under the nature of things, giving the general-truth sense (「人は間違えるものだ」). Since “that's how it should be,” saying it to someone becomes advice based on common sense, “you should ...” (「目上の人には敬語を使うものだ」). And said about something right in front of you, “so that's how things are,” it becomes an exclamation after seeing things anew, giving the feeling sense (「時間がたつのは早いものだ」). All three uses come from the same core idea, “the true nature of things.”

title: 〜もの・〜もん (excuses)
meaning: Used at the end of a sentence to give a reason, to justify yourself or to sound a little childish: “but ...!” / “because ..., that's why!”.
connection: Plain form + もの／もん (often paired with 「だって」)

senses.label: Excuse / pouting
senses.meaning: Gives a reason to defend yourself, with a pouty or defiant tone. Like “because ..., okay?”. Used mostly by women and children, or between close people. Often paired with 「だって」.
senses.connection: Verb / adjective plain form; noun / な-adjective + だ + もの・もん (common: 〜んだもん)
examples: But I didn't know!
“Why aren't you eating?” “I'm not hungry yet!”
I just don't want to go. What can I do?

senses.label: Stressing that it's natural
senses.meaning: Gives a reason to show that something is only natural. Like “after all, ...”. You can use it to explain for someone else, or to insist on your own position.
senses.connection: Plain form + もの／もん; polite feminine form: 「〜ですもの」
examples: No wonder he's angry. You broke your promise, after all.
You don't need to worry. I'm not a kid anymore.
Well, it's the truth, after all.

notes: It has a coaxing, petulant tone, and used to a superior or customer or in a formal setting it sounds childish and irresponsible: ✕「資料が間に合いませんでした。忙しかったんだもん」→ ○「申し訳ありません。立て込んでおりまして、間に合いませんでした」.
Adult men using 「〜もん」 sound childish; even adults use it only with family, a partner, or very close friends.
Nouns and な-adjectives need 「だ」 or 「なんだ」: ✕「子供もん」「好きもん」→ ○「子供だもん」「好きなんだもん」.
The sentence-final 「もの／もん」 gives only the reason and leaves the conclusion, “so don't blame me,” to the listener. If you need to go on to a result, use 「〜ものだから」 or 「〜もので」.

daily.title: A child pouting
daily.description: A child doesn't want to go home yet.
daily.example: No! I still want to play!

daily.title: Explaining why you're late
daily.description: Making excuses to a friend after arriving late.
daily.example: Sorry I'm late. The train had stopped!

daily.title: Between partners
daily.description: Giving a reason in a sweet, pouty way.
daily.example: Well, I wanted to see you!

work.title: Watching dramas, reading manga
work.description: Characters in Japanese dramas and manga often use 「もん」 to sound childish or cute.
work.example: But I like you, that's why!

work.title: A kindergarten teacher listening
work.description: At kindergarten, a child explains a fight to the teacher.
work.example: But Teacher, Taro pushed me first!

etymology: It's generally thought to come from shortening phrases like 「ものだから」 or 「ものを」, leaving only the reason at the end. 「もん」 is a casual sound change of 「もの」.

similar.title: 〜ものだから
similar.explanation: Same origin: the sentence-final 「もの／もん」 is generally thought to be 「ものだから」 with the second half dropped. 「ものだから」 is followed by a result (「忙しかったものだから、行けなかった」) and can be used in fairly formal apologies; the sentence-final 「もん」 leaves only the reason and is more colloquial and more coaxing.

similar.title: 〜もので
similar.explanation: Same origin, close in meaning: 「〜もので」 and 「〜ものですから」 are also excuses meaning “because ... (I couldn't help it),” but with a polite tone that can be used to superiors (「電車が遅れたもので…」); the sentence-final 「もん」 is only for people you are close to.

similar.title: 〜から (cause / reason)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「〜から」 is a neutral statement of cause usable in any setting; 「〜もん」 states the reason while adding a coaxing, defiant tone of “you have to understand me.”

formation: The sentence-final 「もの」 is generally thought to come from phrases like 「ものだから」 or 「ものを」 with the second half dropped. 「もの」 packages the reason as “that's just how things are,” and then the sentence breaks off right at the reason, leaving the conclusion (“so don't blame me / so it can't be helped”) for the listener to infer. Giving only the reason while asking for understanding creates a coaxing, petulant tone. It is often paired with 「だって」 (“but”), forming an excuse frame of “but ..., you know.” 「もん」 is the colloquial sound change of 「もの」, and sounds even more casual and childlike.

meaning: Gives a personal reason, often as an excuse, with the feeling “that's how it was, I couldn't help it”: “because ..., so ...”.
connection: Plain form (noun / な-adjective + な) + ものだから (casual: もんだから; polite: ものですから)

senses.label: Excuse
senses.meaning: Explains the reason for your mistake or for something you couldn't avoid, with the tone “that's how it was, it couldn't be helped”. The second clause is usually a bad result or an apology.
senses.connection: Verb / い-adjective plain form + ものだから／ものですから
examples: The roads were jammed, so I ended up late.
My alarm clock didn't go off, so I overslept.

senses.label: So ... that ...
senses.meaning: Something is so extreme that the result follows naturally. Like “it was so ... that ...”. Often used with 「あまり」, 「あんまり」, or 「とても」.
senses.connection: (あまり／あんまり) + plain form + ものだから
examples: It was so hot that I fell asleep with the air conditioner on.
My child was crying so much that I couldn't help picking them up.
She was so serious that I couldn't say a thing.

notes: The second clause can't be a command, request, or invitation: ✕「寒いものだから、窓を閉めてください」→ ○「寒いので、窓を閉めていただけますか」.

In Japan, giving the reason first when you are late or have made a mistake is taken as making excuses. To a superior or customer, apologize first and then add the reason with 「ものですから」: ○「申し訳ありません。電車が遅れたものですから…」.
Nouns and な-adjectives take 「な」: ✕「学生だものだから」→ ○「学生なものだから」; ○「好きなものだから」.
It carries a personal excuse tone of “I couldn't help it,” so it isn't used in objective reports or explanatory writing: ✕「気温が上がったものだから、氷が溶けた」 (a scientific explanation) → ○「気温が上がったため、氷が溶けた」.

daily.title: Excuse for being late
daily.description: Explaining to a friend why you were late.
daily.example: Sorry, I overslept.

daily.title: Explaining why you didn't reply
daily.description: A friend asks why you didn't answer their message.
daily.example: My phone battery died, so I couldn't get in touch.

work.title: Apologizing to a client
work.description: Explaining a late email reply to a client.
work.example: Due to a system problem, our reply was delayed.

work.title: Explaining to your boss
work.description: Telling your boss why you were late for a meeting.
work.example: My train was delayed, so I was a little late for the meeting.

etymology: Made of the formal noun 「もの」 + 「だ」 + 「から」 (reason). 「もの」 presents the reason as an established fact, which gives the excuse-like tone “it already happened, nothing could be done”.

similar.title: 〜もので
similar.explanation: Same origin, close in meaning: 「〜もので」 means the same as 「〜ものだから」 and is mostly used in polite excuses and apologies, a bit more compact and written than 「ものだから」.

similar.title: 〜ので
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「ので」 is objective and soft, and the second clause can take a request (「寒いので、窓を閉めてください」); 「ものだから」 stresses “circumstances forced my hand” and is used to excuse yourself, so the second clause can't take a request.

similar.title: 〜から (cause / reason)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「から」 is an ordinary statement of cause, and the second clause can use a command or request; 「ものだから」 carries an excuse tone, and the second clause can only be a result that has already happened or your own action.

similar.title: 〜もの・〜もん (excuse)
similar.explanation: Same origin: drop the second half of 「ものだから」 and put it at the end of the sentence, and it becomes the more colloquial, more coaxing 「〜もの／もん」 (「だって、忙しかったんだもん」).

formation: 「〜ものだから」 = the formal noun 「もの」 + the copula 「だ」 + the reason particle 「から」. 「ものだ」 presents the first clause as an established state of affairs, “that's just how things are,” and 「から」 then uses it as the reason: “since that's how things stand, ...” Because the reason is presented as something unchangeable, the implication is “I didn't do it on purpose; I couldn't help it,” and that is where the excuse tone comes from. When used with 「あまり」 or 「とても」, the high degree is treated as something unstoppable, which naturally leads to the consequence. Since the point is “it was out of my hands,” the second clause cannot be a command or request the speaker actively directs at someone.

meaning: Uses a fact both sides know as a reason, stressing “since ..., (you should) ...”. Usually followed by an opinion, a demand, or a conclusion.
connection: Plain form (noun / な-adjective + な) + のだから (casual: んだから)

senses.label: Since ..., then ...
senses.meaning: The first part is a settled fact that the listener also knows. The second part is an opinion, order, advice, or conclusion based on it. Like “since ..., (then) ...”. Fairly strong; it's meant to persuade.
senses.connection: Plain form + のだから／んだから + command / advice / intention / conclusion
examples: You're an adult now, so take care of your own things.
You promised, so keep your word.
Since you've come all this way, please stay and relax.

senses.label: Sentence-final complaint
senses.meaning: 「〜んだから」 alone at the end of a sentence complains about someone, with exasperation or mild reproach. Like “honestly, you always ...!”. Often used with 「もう」, 「本当に」, or 「まったく」.
senses.connection: Plain form + んだから。(at the end of the sentence; the rest is left unsaid)
examples: Honestly, you're always late.
You forgot your phone again? You're so forgetful.

notes: It carries a pushy tone of “this is a fact you know too, so you ought to ...” Saying 「部長なんですから、決めてください」 to a superior feels like pressuring them, which is very rude.

It points the opposite way from 「〜ものだから」: 「のだから」 uses a fact to make demands of the listener, while 「ものだから」 makes excuses for yourself. When apologizing, ✕「寝坊したのだから、遅れました」 sounds like a brazen excuse → ○「寝坊したものですから、遅れてしまいました」.
The sentence-final 「〜んだから」 on its own is a complaint or reproach (「また忘れたの？本当にだらしないんだから」), and is used only with family or close friends.
The first clause must be an established fact, not a hypothesis: ✕「もし雨なのだから、中止しよう」→ ○「雨なのだから、中止しよう」／「もし雨なら、中止しよう」.

daily.title: A parent nagging
daily.description: A parent tells their high schooler to get up earlier.
daily.example: You're in high school now. Get yourself up.

daily.title: Encouraging a friend
daily.description: Your friend is nervous before a competition, so you cheer them on.
daily.example: You practiced so hard, so be confident.

daily.title: Grumbling at family
daily.description: Someone left the lights on again, and you can't help grumbling.
daily.example: The lights are on again. Honestly, it's always like this.

work.title: A boss encouraging a team member
work.description: Before a big presentation, a boss cheers on a team member.
work.example: You've prepared this much, so it'll definitely go well.

work.title: Making a proposal in a meeting
work.description: The budget is limited, so you suggest setting priorities.
work.example: Since our budget is limited, let's set priorities and move forward.

etymology: Made of 「のだ」, which explains or confirms a fact, plus 「から」 (reason). 「のだ」 confirms the first part as an established fact, which gives the sense “since ...”. 「んだから」 is the casual sound change.

similar.title: 〜からには
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean “since ..., then ...” 「からには」 is usually followed by determination or duty to see it through, in a more solemn, stronger tone (「引き受けたからには、最後までやる」); 「のだから」 focuses on persuading the other person with a fact you both know.

similar.title: 〜以上(は)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「以上は」 also means “since ..., then ...,” is more written, and is mostly used for duty and resolve (「約束した以上は守るべきだ」); 「のだから」 is more colloquial and often used for persuading or reproaching.

similar.title: 〜のだ・〜んです
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「のだから」 is simply 「のだ」 + 「から」. 「のだ」 by itself explains or confirms a situation; adding 「から」 treats the confirmed fact as the reason, which produces the “since ...” tone.

similar.title: 〜から (cause / reason)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「から」 just states an ordinary cause, and can give new information; with 「のだから」 the first clause is a fact the other person also knows, and the tone is persuading or reproaching.

formation: 「〜のだから」 = 「のだ」 + the reason particle 「から」. 「のだ」 confirms something as “just the fact,” and 「から」 then takes that fact as grounds: “since that fact is right there, then ...” Because the grounds are a fact the other person can't deny either, the second clause is often a request, advice, or a conclusion, which is very persuasive but also feels pushy. If you drop the second clause and end with just 「〜んだから」, it becomes “well, that's how it is (you're always like this),” leaving the conclusion to the listener, and it turns into a complaint or a scolding. 「んだから」 is the colloquial form of 「のだから」.

meaning: State your conclusion first, then give the reason with 「なぜなら」, usually ending with 「〜からだ」: “because ...” / “the reason is ...”.
connection: Conclusion. なぜなら(ば) + plain form + からだ／ためだ

senses.label: Adding the reason
senses.meaning: State a conclusion or claim, then explain the reason in the next sentence. Like “This is because ...”. Formal and logical. Common in essays, speeches, and arguments.
senses.connection: Conclusion. なぜなら(ば)、〜からだ／〜からです／〜からである
examples: I disagree with his opinion. That's because his approach is too dangerous.
I'm leaving early today. The reason is that it's my child's birthday.
This hypothesis does not hold. This is because the data are contradictory.

senses.label: Spoken versions
senses.meaning: 「なぜかというと」 and 「どうしてかというと」 are more conversational. Same meaning, but softer than 「なぜなら」.
senses.connection: なぜかというと／どうしてかというと、〜からだ(です)
examples: I'm studying Japanese. The reason is that I love Japanese anime.
I'm never going to that shop again. Why? Because the staff were rude.

notes: 「なぜなら」 comes after the conclusion and starts a new sentence stating the reason; it can't be put inside the reason clause: ✕「なぜなら雨だから、行かない」→ ○「行かない。なぜなら、雨だからだ」.
End the sentence with a matching 「からだ」, 「ためだ」, or 「のだ」, not just 「ので」 or nothing at all: ✕「なぜなら、雨が降ったので。」→ ○「なぜなら、雨が降ったからだ」.
The tone is that of a debate or a paper. In everyday conversation, answering 「どうして？」 with 「なぜなら〜」 sounds stiff and preachy; the natural forms are 「〜からです」 and 「実は〜んです」.

daily.title: Writing an essay
daily.description: A student writes about their dream and the reason for it.
daily.example: My dream is to become a doctor. That's because I want to help sick people.

daily.title: Giving a friend a tip
daily.description: A friend asks about a movie, and you explain why you'd skip it.
daily.example: You'd better not watch that movie. Why? Because the ending is really sad.

work.title: Explaining a proposal
work.description: Recommending a plan in a meeting and giving the reason.
work.example: I recommend this plan. The reason is that it has the lowest cost.

work.title: Writing a paper
work.description: Arguing for a conclusion in an academic paper.
work.example: This method is not practical. This is because it takes too much time.

etymology: Made of the question word 「なぜ」 (“why”) plus 「なら(ば)」, the conditional form of 「だ」. Literally: “if you ask why”. It brings in the reason by asking and answering its own question, just like 「なぜかというと」.

similar.title: 〜のは〜からだ
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both end with 「からだ」 to explain a reason. 「のは〜からだ」 makes the result the topic and the reason the focus within a single sentence; 「なぜなら」 finishes the conclusion first and then adds the reason in a separate sentence.

similar.title: 〜というのも〜からだ
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: it also adds the reason after the fact, but in a lighter tone, often to give background or inside circumstances (「最近忙しい。というのも、引っ越したからだ」); 「なぜなら」 is more like logical argument.

similar.title: 〜から (cause / reason)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「から」 usually puts the reason clause first (「雨だから行かない」); 「なぜなら〜からだ」 puts the reason after the conclusion as a separate explanation, stressing the reason more.

formation: 「なぜなら」 = the interrogative 「なぜ」 (“why”) + 「なら（ば）」 (the conditional of the copula 「だ」, “if you ask ...”), literally “if you ask why.” The speaker first raises the “why” on the listener's behalf and then answers it, a self-question-and-answer structure. Since what follows answers “why,” the answer naturally closes with 「〜からだ」 (“it is because ...”), so the two appear as a pair. Giving the conclusion first, then the self-posed question, then the reason lays the steps of the reasoning out in the open, so it sounds logical and rather written. 「なぜかというと」 and 「どうしてかというと」 have the same structure, only more colloquial.

meaning: Presents a result or situation as the topic, then gives the reason at the end: “The reason ... is that ...”.
connection: Plain form (noun / な-adjective + な) + のは + reason (plain form) + からだ／ためだ

senses.label: Explaining the reason
senses.meaning: The result goes before 「のは」 as the topic, and the reason comes at the end as the focus. Like “The reason ... is that ...”. Puts more weight on the reason than 「〜から、〜」 does.
senses.connection: 〜のは、plain form + からだ／からです
examples: The reason I was late is that the train stopped.
He's popular because he's kind to everyone.
I came to Japan because I love Japanese culture.

senses.label: Written style: ためだ
senses.meaning: In writing, news, and reports, 「〜のは〜ためだ／ためである」 is common. Same meaning, but more formal.
senses.connection: 〜のは、verb / adjective plain form or noun + の + ためだ／ためである
examples: The accident occurred because the checks were insufficient.
Vegetable prices went up because there was little rain.

notes: The first half must nominalize the action with 「の」 before 「は」: ✕「遅刻したは、電車が止まったからだ」→ ○「遅刻したのは、電車が止まったからだ」.
When a noun or な-adjective is the reason, add 「だ」: ✕「好きからです」→ ○「好きだからです」.

In 「〜のは〜ためだ」, 「ため」 after the た-form or a state is a cause, but after the dictionary form of a volitional verb it is a purpose: 「来たのは、雨が降ったためだ」 (cause) ↔ 「来たのは、日本語を勉強するためだ」 (purpose). Don't mix them up.
When explaining a mistake to a superior, opening with 「遅れたのは、電車が止まったからです」 sounds like shifting the blame. Apologize first, then explain the reason.

daily.title: Explaining to a friend
daily.description: A friend asks why you missed yesterday's get-together.
daily.example: The reason I couldn't come yesterday is that I had a fever.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: The news explains why prices are rising.
daily.example: Prices are rising because the yen keeps getting weaker.

work.title: Reporting results
work.description: Explaining to your boss why sales went up.
work.example: Sales grew because the new product was well received.

work.title: Explaining a delay to a client
work.description: Telling a client why the delivery was late.
work.example: The delivery was late because the parts arrived late.

etymology: Made of the formal noun 「の」, the topic particle 「は」, and the statement 「〜からだ」 (reason + だ). It's a “cleft sentence”: the reason you want to stress goes in the focus position at the end.

similar.title: なぜなら〜からだ
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「なぜなら」 finishes the conclusion and then adds the reason in a separate sentence; 「のは〜からだ」 does it all in one sentence, with the reason as the focus of the sentence.

similar.title: 〜というのも〜からだ
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both use 「からだ」 at the end to give the reason. 「というのも」 follows the previous sentence and supplies background or inside circumstances; 「のは〜からだ」 makes the result itself the topic and then explains the reason.

similar.title: 〜のは〜だ (emphasis)
similar.explanation: Same origin: the same cleft-sentence frame. 「のは〜だ」 can emphasize any element, such as a person, thing, or time (「来たのは田中さんだ」); 「のは〜からだ」 is specifically for putting the reason in the focus position.

similar.title: 〜から (cause / reason)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: in 「AからB」 the reason comes first and the result second, so the point of information is the result; rewritten as 「BのはAからだ」, the emphasis shifts to the reason.

formation: 「〜のは〜からだ」 has three parts: the formal noun 「の」 turns the sentence stating the result into a noun phrase; the topic particle 「は」 makes it the topic; and the sentence-final 「〜からだ」 (reason + copula) is the predicate. In an ordinary 「AからB」 the reason is just a subordinate clause; rewritten as 「BのはAからだ」, the reason moves to the predicate position at the end. In Japanese the end of the sentence is the focus of information, so the reason is highlighted, and the meaning becomes “the reason B is that A.” This structure is called a cleft sentence, the same frame as the emphatic 「〜のは〜だ」, only with the reason as the focus.

meaning: Shows the outcome reached after an action or process: “as a result of ...” / “after ..., in the end ...”.
connection: Verb た-form / noun + の + 結果(、)

senses.label: As a result of ...
senses.meaning: The first part is an action that took some process; the second part is the outcome. Like “as a result of ...”. Often used with 「調べる」, 「話し合う」, 「検討する」, or 「努力する」. Common in writing, news, and reports.
senses.connection: Verb た-form + 結果、／noun + の + 結果、
examples: After talking it over with my family, I decided to study abroad.
The checkup found nothing abnormal.
As a result of practicing every day, we were able to win the match.

senses.label: その結果・結果として
senses.meaning: 「その結果」 at the start of a sentence follows on from the cause in the previous sentence. 「結果として」 and 「結果的に」 mean “in the end; as a result”.
senses.connection: (Previous sentence). その結果、〜／結果として、〜
examples: He studied late every day. As a result, he got into his first-choice school.
The talks reached no agreement, and in the end the plan was canceled.

notes: The second clause is an outcome that has already appeared, so it can't take an intention, command, or request: ✕「よく考えた結果、決めてください」→ ○「よく考えてから決めてください」.
A verb must be in the た-form, and a noun needs 「の」: ✕「調べる結果、〜」→ ○「調べた結果、〜」; ✕「検査結果、〜」 as a connector → ○「検査の結果、〜」.

「結果的に」 carries the nuance “it wasn't the aim, but it turned out this way.” Using it to evaluate someone's results (「結果的にうまくいきましたね」) can be heard as “it only worked out by luck,” so be careful with superiors and customers.

daily.title: Losing weight
daily.description: Telling a friend how your diet went.
daily.example: After rethinking what I eat, I lost three kilos.

daily.title: Comparison shopping
daily.description: Finally deciding after comparing several models.
daily.example: After comparing all kinds of options, I went with this computer.

work.title: News report
work.description: The news reports the findings of a fire investigation.
work.example: A police investigation found that the fire was caused by an electric heater.

work.title: Meeting decision
work.description: Informing someone of a decision after review.
work.example: After internal review, we have decided not to proceed with your proposal this time.

etymology: 「結果」 is a Sino-Japanese word that first meant “(a plant) bearing fruit”, and later “the final outcome of something”. Grammatically, it follows an action to mean “the outcome reached after doing ...”.

similar.title: 〜末(に)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean “after ..., finally ...” 「末に」 stresses that the result came after long agonizing or repeated trying (「悩んだ末に、退職を決めた」); 「結果」 is more neutral and objective, often used in reports and news.

similar.title: 〜あげく
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「あげく」 also gives the outcome after a process, but mostly a bad one, with a note of dissatisfaction or regret (「さんざん迷ったあげく、何も買わなかった」); 「結果」 can be good or bad.

similar.title: 〜たところ (result)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「たところ」 expresses a fact discovered by chance after doing something, often with a sense of surprise (「聞いてみたところ、もう売り切れだった」); 「た結果」 is the outcome after a deliberate process.

formation: 「結果」 is itself a noun; its original meaning is a plant “bearing fruit,” extended to “the final outcome of something.” In Japanese a noun can be modified directly by a verb in the attributive form, so 「話し合った結果」 is “the fruit that the discussion bore.” The た-form is required because the action must be completed before there can be any “fruit” from it; with a noun, the usual noun-modifies-noun rule applies and 「の」 is added. The whole 「〜た結果」 is placed at the start of the sentence as an adverbial, followed by 「、」, to introduce the main clause, so that clause is naturally an outcome that has become fact, never an intention or a command.

meaning: A partial or soft denial: “it's not that ...” / “not (all) ...”.
connection: Plain form (noun + な／である; な-adjective + な) + わけではない (casual: わけじゃない)

senses.label: Partial denial
senses.meaning: Denies the idea that something is “all” or “always” so. Like “not necessarily ...” or “not all ...”. Often used with 「全部」, 「いつも」, 「みんな」, or 「必ずしも」.
senses.connection: (全部／いつも／必ずしも) + plain form + わけではない
examples: Expensive restaurants aren't always good.
Not all Japanese people like sushi.
Having money doesn't necessarily make you happy, either.

senses.label: Soft denial
senses.meaning: Denies a conclusion the listener might naturally draw from what was said or from the situation. Like “it's not that ...”. Soft in tone; often followed by 「が／けど」 and what you really think. Often used with 「別に」 or 「特に」.
senses.connection: (別に) + plain form + わけではない／わけじゃない
examples: It's not that I don't like it. I just don't feel like eating it today.
I'm not angry or anything.
It's not that I'm against it, but I'm a little worried.

notes: It resembles 「〜わけがない」, but the one particle makes the meaning completely different: 「彼が犯人なわけではない」 (I'm not saying he's the culprit) ↔ 「彼が犯人なわけがない」 (there's no way he's the culprit).
It is also completely different from 「〜わけにはいかない」: 「行かないわけではない」 (it's not that I won't go) ↔ 「行かないわけにはいかない」 (I can't not go).
Nouns and な-adjectives need 「な」 or 「という」: ✕「学生わけではない」→ ○「学生なわけではない」／「学生というわけではない」.

Japanese speakers often use 「〜わけではないんですが…」 to refuse or voice dissatisfaction indirectly, and the real meaning is often in the second half (「嫌いなわけじゃないんですが、今日はちょっと…」 = I don't feel like it today). Pay attention to what comes after.

daily.title: Softly turning down an invitation
daily.description: A friend invites you out, and you explain it's not that you don't want to go.
daily.example: It's not that I don't want to go. I just have something on today.

daily.title: Explaining what you eat
daily.description: Someone asks whether you never eat meat at all.
daily.example: It's not that I can't eat meat at all.

work.title: Voicing reservations in a meeting
work.description: Commenting on a coworker's proposal without sounding opposed.
work.example: It's not that I'm against this plan, but I think it needs a bit more thought.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: A commentator explains that the economy hasn't improved across the board.
work.example: The economy may have recovered, but that doesn't mean every company is doing better.

etymology: 「わけ」 is written 「訳」 and means “reason, logic, circumstances”. 「わけではない」 literally means “that's not the situation; that's not the logic”, so it's used to deny an inference or a sweeping statement.

similar.title: 〜とは限らない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning (partial negation): 「とは限らない」 stresses “not necessarily, there are exceptions” and is mostly used for general rules (「高いものがいいとは限らない」); 「わけではない」 can also deny the other person's guess or misunderstanding.

similar.title: 必ずしも〜ない・必ずしも〜とは限らない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning (partial negation): 「必ずしも〜ない」 is an adverb-matching construction and more written; it is often used together with 「わけではない」: 「必ずしも正しいわけではない」.

similar.title: 〜わけだ
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「わけだ」 means “following the logic, this is the conclusion” (「だから安いわけだ」); 「わけではない」 denies exactly that kind of conclusion.

similar.title: 〜わけがない
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「わけがない」 means “there's no reason for that,” a strong denial of possibility (“there's no way”); 「わけではない」 only denies partially or gently, and is much weaker.

formation: 「〜わけではない」 = 「わけ」 (訳: reason, circumstances, conclusion) + 「では」 + 「ない」. 「〜わけだ」 means “following the logic, this is the conclusion,” and adding 「ではない」 denies not the fact itself but “that conclusion, that sweeping way of putting it.” So 「嫌いなわけではない」 doesn't mean “I like it”; it means “you can't conclude from this that I dislike it.” When what is denied is an inference like “all” or “always,” it becomes a partial negation; when it is the other person's guess, it becomes a gentle denial. The 「は」 in 「では」 limits the negation to “this conclusion” and hints that “other aspects are another matter,” so it is often followed by 「が／けど」 to state the real feeling.

meaning: Shows a feeling, sensation, or desire so strong you can't control it: “so ... I can't help it” / “extremely ...”.
connection: Verb te-form / い-adjective くて / な-adjective で + しょうがない・仕方がない

senses.label: Strong feeling / sensation
senses.meaning: With words for feelings or sensations, shows a degree so strong you can't do anything about it. Like “terribly ...” or “so ... I can't help it”. Common with 「うれしい」, 「心配」, 「眠い」, 「痛い」, and 「寂しい」.
senses.connection: い-adjective くて / な-adjective で + しょうがない・仕方がない
examples: My head has been killing me since this morning.
I'm terribly worried about tomorrow's exam.
I've just started living alone, and I'm so lonely.

senses.label: Desire / can't stop thinking
senses.meaning: With 「〜たくて」 or verbs like 「気になる」, shows that you really want to do something, or can't stop thinking about it.
senses.connection: Verb ます-stem + たくて / verb te-form + しょうがない・仕方がない
examples: I'm dying to go on a trip.
I couldn't stop thinking about what he said.

notes: It resembles 「〜てもしょうがない」, but the single 「も」 changes the meaning completely: 「心配でしょうがない」 (I'm worried sick) ↔ 「心配してもしょうがない」 (there's no use worrying).
The subject is normally the speaker. For other people, add 「ようだ」 or 「らしい」, or use 「〜がる」: ✕「彼は寂しくてしょうがない」→ ○「彼は寂しくてしょうがないようだ」／「彼は寂しがっている」.
「しょうがない」 is very colloquial; to superiors and customers use 「〜て仕方がありません」, and in formal writing 「〜てならない」 is more common.

daily.title: Looking forward to a trip
daily.description: The day before a trip, you tell a friend how excited you are.
daily.example: My trip starts tomorrow, and I can't wait.

daily.title: Hay fever season
daily.description: Complaining to your family when spring hay fever kicks in.
daily.example: My hay fever is making my eyes itch like crazy.

daily.title: Talking about grandchildren
daily.description: An older person chats with a neighbor about their grandchild.
daily.example: My grandchild is just too adorable.

work.title: Waiting for results
work.description: After presenting a proposal, you tell a coworker how you feel.
work.example: I can't stop wondering how my presentation went.

work.title: After an all-nighter
work.description: Grumbling quietly at the office after working through the night.
work.example: I pulled an all-nighter, and I'm so sleepy.

etymology: 「仕方」 means “way of doing”, so 「仕方がない」 means “there's no way (to deal with it)”. 「しょうがない」 is a sound change of 「しようがない」 (仕様がない). After a feeling word, it means “the feeling is so strong I can't do anything about it”.

similar.title: 〜てたまらない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: the two are often interchangeable. 「てたまらない」 stresses a more bodily, emotional feeling of “can't stand it”; 「てしょうがない」 is more colloquial and is also often used for uncontrollable states like 「気になって」.

similar.title: 〜てならない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「てならない」 is more written, and mostly follows words like 「気がする」, 「思える」, and 「心配だ」, spontaneous feelings that well up of their own accord (「何か起きる気がしてならない」).

similar.title: 〜てもしょうがない・〜ても仕方がない
similar.explanation: Same origin: also built from 「しょうがない／仕方がない」 (“there's nothing to be done”). With the added concessive 「も」, the meaning becomes “it's no use ...” or “no wonder ...”

formation: 「〜てしょうがない」 = the て-form (cause or state) + 「しょうがない／仕方がない」 (“there's nothing to be done”). Literally, “because of ..., I can't do anything about it”: 「心配で仕方がない」 = “I'm so worried that I can't help it (can't control it).” What you can do nothing about is your own feeling or sensation, so the meaning becomes a feeling so strong you can't control it, “... like crazy.” Since it describes an inner feeling the speaker can't control, the subject is usually the first person, and what precedes is mostly words for feelings, sensations, and desires. 「しょうがない」 is a sound change of 「しようがない」 (仕様がない), more colloquial than 「仕方がない」.

meaning: Shows a feeling, sensation, or desire so strong it's hard to bear: “unbearably ...” / “so ... I can't stand it”.
connection: Verb te-form / い-adjective くて / な-adjective で + たまらない

senses.label: Strong sensation / feeling
senses.meaning: With words for sensations or feelings, shows a degree too strong to bear. Like “unbearably ...” or “terribly ...”. Common with 「暑い」, 「痛い」, 「うれしい」, and 「心配」.
senses.connection: い-adjective くて / な-adjective で + たまらない／たまりません
examples: It's unbearably hot today.
I passed the exam, and I'm overjoyed.
My tooth hurts so much I can't stand it.

senses.label: Strong desire
senses.meaning: With 「〜たくて」, or with phrases like 「おなかがすく」 or 「のどが渇く」, shows a strong want or need.
senses.connection: Verb ます-stem + たくて / verb te-form + たまらない
examples: I'm dying to see my family back home.
I was terribly thirsty.

notes: The subject is normally the speaker. For other people, use 「〜てたまらないようだ」, 「〜てたまらないらしい」, or 「〜がっている」: ✕「妹は国に帰りたくてたまらない」→ ○「妹は国に帰りたがっている」.
It expresses only the speaker's own sensation or feeling, not an objective property: ✕「この部屋は広くてたまらない」.
On its own, 「たまらない」 is often praise, “so good I can't stand it”: 「この味がたまらない」 = this taste is fantastic, not “I can't stand this taste.” Reading it only literally gets the meaning backward.

daily.title: Broken air conditioner in summer
daily.description: Complaining to your family about the heat.
daily.example: The air conditioner broke, and it's unbearably hot.

daily.title: Homesick abroad
daily.description: A student abroad tells a friend how much they miss home.
daily.example: It's been six months since I came to study here, and I'm dying to see my family.

daily.title: Starving
daily.description: You come home from school starving.
daily.example: I'm starving. Let's eat something.

work.title: Waiting for interview results
work.description: After an interview, you tell a friend how anxious you are.
work.example: I can't stop thinking about the interview results.

work.title: Overtime day after day
work.description: Complaining to a coworker after working late every day.
work.example: After working overtime day after day, I'm unbearably sleepy.

etymology: 「たまる」 is written 「堪る」 and means “to bear, to endure”. Today it's almost only used in the negative. 「たまらない」 means “can't bear it”. After a feeling or sensation, it shows a degree too strong to endure.

similar.title: 〜てしょうがない・〜て仕方がない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: the two are often interchangeable. 「てたまらない」 stresses a physical, emotional feeling of “can't bear it”; 「てしょうがない」 is more colloquial and is also often used for uncontrollable states like 「気になって」.

similar.title: 〜てならない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「てならない」 is more written, mostly used for feelings that well up naturally such as 「気がしてならない」 and 「思えてならない」, and is generally not used for physical pain or heat.

similar.title: 〜ずにはいられない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean “can't help it.” 「てたまらない」 describes a state of feeling or sensation (「おかしくてたまらない」); 「ずにはいられない」 describes an act you can't keep yourself from doing (「笑わずにはいられない」).

formation: 「〜てたまらない」 = the て-form (cause or state) + 「たまらない」. 「たまる」 is written 「堪る」 and means “to endure, to hold out”; in modern Japanese it is almost only used in the negative, so 「たまらない」 means “can't hold out, can't stand it.” Put together, 「暑くてたまらない」 = “it's so hot I can't stand it.” Because the core idea is “can't endure,” it carries a more physical, emotional sense of “being overwhelmed” than 「〜てしょうがない」, and the one enduring is usually the speaker. Being knocked flat by delicious food or charm is also a kind of “can't stand it,” which is why 「たまらない」 on its own can also be a compliment, “irresistibly good.”

meaning: Driven by feelings or circumstances, you can't stop yourself from doing something: “can't help ...ing”.
connection: Verb ない-form (drop ない) + ずにはいられない (する → せずにはいられない)

senses.label: Can't help it
senses.meaning: A strong emotion makes you do something naturally. Like “can't help ...ing”. Common with 「笑う」, 「泣く」, and 「感動する」.
senses.connection: Verb ない-form + ずにはいられない／ずにはいられなかった
examples: I couldn't help crying when I watched that movie.
When I heard his joke, I couldn't help laughing.

senses.label: An urge you must act on
senses.meaning: An inner urge, such as a sense of duty or worry, makes you feel you have to do something. Like “I have to ...” or “I can't not ...”.
senses.connection: Verb ない-form + ずにはいられない (common: 言わずには, 確かめずには)
examples: When I spot a mistake, I can't help pointing it out.
I'm so worried that I can't help checking again and again.
On this issue, I have to say something.

notes: 「する」 becomes 「せず」: ✕「しずにはいられない」→ ○「心配せずにはいられない」.
It means “can't help doing it,” not “must do it (obligation)”: 「一言言わずにはいられない」 means “I can't help saying a word.” For rules and obligations use 「〜なければならない」.
The subject is normally the speaker; for others add 「ようだ」 or 「らしい」. When the subject is a thing and the meaning is “inevitably causes ...,” use 「〜ずにはおかない」: ✕「この映画は人を感動させずにはいられない」→ ○「感動させずにはおかない」.

daily.title: Watching disaster news
daily.description: Seeing reports from a disaster area makes you want to help.
daily.example: When I see news from the disaster area, I can't help wanting to do something.

daily.title: Watching a match
daily.description: Telling a friend how you reacted the moment a goal was scored.
daily.example: The moment the goal went in, I couldn't help shouting.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: You couldn't put the novel down.
daily.example: I had to know how it ended, so I couldn't stop until I'd read to the very end.

work.title: Speaking up at a meeting
work.description: Formally raising an opinion at an official meeting.
work.example: On this matter, I feel I must say a word.

work.title: Writing a book review
work.description: Describing your impressions in a review.
work.example: Reading this book, you can't help thinking about how you live your own life.

etymology: Made of 「ずに」, from the classical negative 「ず」, plus the particle 「は」 and 「いられない」, the negative potential form of 「いる」. Literally: “can't stay without doing”, hence “can't help doing”.

similar.title: 〜ないではいられない
similar.explanation: Same origin, same meaning: 「ず」 and 「ない」 are both negatives, so the meaning is identical; only the connection differs (「泣かずには」 ↔ 「泣かないでは」). 「ないでは」 is a little more colloquial.

similar.title: 〜ずにはおかない／〜ないではおかない
similar.explanation: Same origin: also a double negative of the form 「ずには＋negative」. 「ずにはおかない」 often has a thing as its subject, meaning “inevitably causes ...,” or expresses the speaker's resolve that “I will definitely ...”; 「ずにはいられない」 is the speaker being unable to help themselves.

similar.title: 〜てたまらない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean “can't help it.” 「てたまらない」 describes a state of feeling or sensation; 「ずにはいられない」 describes an act you can't keep yourself from doing.

similar.title: 〜てしまう
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「つい〜てしまう」 means doing something without realizing it, with the stress on the result and regret (「つい食べてしまった」); 「ずにはいられない」 stresses an uncontrollable strong urge.

formation: 「〜ずにはいられない」 has four parts: the literary negative 「ず」 (= ない) + 「に」 make 「ずに」, “in the state of not doing ...”; the topic particle 「は」 singles out that state; and 「いられない」, the negative potential of 「いる」 (“to stay, to remain in a state”), means “can't keep on.” Put together: “in a state of not doing ..., I can't stay.” If you can't stay without doing it, you have to do it, and since this “have to” comes from an inner urge rather than an external rule, the meaning is “can't help but, can't resist.” Because it is an inner urge, the subject is usually the first person.

meaning: What's done is done, and doing something now won't solve anything: “there's no use ...ing” / “it won't help to ...”.
connection: Verb te-form + も始まらない (casual: 〜たって始まらない)

senses.label: No use
senses.meaning: Doing something is pointless and won't fix the problem. Like “it's no use ...ing”. Often used with 「今さら」 or 「いつまでも」, and often followed by a suggestion of what to do instead.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + も始まらない (common: 後悔しても, 悩んでいても, 嘆いても)
examples: It's no use having regrets now.
Worrying about it alone won't get you anywhere. Why not talk to someone?

senses.label: Casual and polite forms
senses.meaning: In casual speech, 「〜たって始まらない」. In polite speech, 「〜ても始まりません」. Same meaning.
senses.connection: Verb た-form + って + 始まらない / verb te-form + も + 始まりません
examples: Complaining won't help. We just have to do it.
There's no use lamenting the past.

notes: It only means “it's no use ...”; it doesn't mean “no wonder”: ✕「約束を破ったのだから、嫌われても始まらない」→ ○「嫌われても仕方がない」.

Saying 「泣いても始まらないよ」 straight to someone who is grieving or has just met with misfortune sounds cold and preachy. It is even worse with superiors and elders; show sympathy first, then encourage them gently.

The first clause is mostly a negative “spinning your wheels” act such as regret, complaining, or crying. With a positive act the meaning doesn't work: ✕「努力しても始まらない」 (unless you mean the ironic “even effort is wasted”).

daily.title: Comforting a heartbroken friend
daily.description: Your friend keeps crying after a breakup, so you urge them to move on.
daily.example: Crying forever won't get you anywhere.

daily.title: Getting lost
daily.description: You and a friend are lost and blaming each other, so you suggest checking the map.
daily.example: Arguing here won't help. Let's look at the map.

work.title: After a failed project
work.description: A boss tells the team to plan the next steps instead of dwelling on regrets.
work.example: There's no use regretting the failure. Let's think about what to do next.

etymology: 「始まる」 means “to begin”. 「〜ても始まらない」 literally means “even if you do ..., nothing gets started”: no progress, wasted effort. From this comes “it's no use”.

similar.title: 〜てもしょうがない・〜ても仕方がない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean “it's no use ...” 「ても仕方がない」 also means “no wonder ...”; 「ても始まらない」 doesn't, and stresses “things don't move forward at all,” often followed by a suggestion of “why not ...”

similar.title: 〜たところで
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「たところで」 also means “even if ..., (it's no use),” is more written, and the second clause is often 「無駄だ」 or 「変わらない」; it is often paired with 「どうせ」 and 「いくら」.

similar.title: 〜ても (even if)
similar.explanation: Same origin: the first half of 「ても始まらない」 is just the concessive 「〜ても」. 「ても」 by itself only means “even if”; it is 「始まらない」 that adds the sense of futility.

formation: 「〜ても始まらない」 = the concessive 「〜ても」 (“even if ...”) + 「始まらない」 (“won't start”). Here 「始まる」 means that things “get moving, make progress,” so 「始まらない」 means “nothing gets started, nothing changes.” Put together: “even if you do ..., things won't get anywhere” → “it's no use.” Since the stress is on “not moving things forward,” the first clause is mostly something like regret or complaining, which keeps you stuck, and what follows is often a suggestion to do something practical, such as 「〜しかない」 or 「〜たら？」.

meaning: Shows that doing something is useless or pointless, or that an outcome is only natural and can't be helped: “there's no point in ...” / “no wonder ...”.
connection: Verb te-form / い-adjective くて / noun・な-adjective で + もしょうがない・も仕方がない

senses.label: No point doing it
senses.meaning: Doing something is pointless and won't change anything. Like “there's no point in ...”. Often followed by a suggestion.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + もしょうがない／も仕方がない
examples: There's no point hurrying now. We won't make it anyway.
There's no point worrying about what's already over.
Thinking about it on my own won't help, so let's ask the teacher.

senses.label: No wonder / can't be helped
senses.meaning: A (bad) result is only natural, and there's nothing to say against it. Like “no wonder ...” or “you can't complain if ...”. Often used with the passive: 「〜と言われても」, 「〜されても」.
senses.connection: Verb passive te-form + も仕方がない (common: 言われても, 嫌われても, 怒られても)
examples: You broke your promise three times, so no wonder they don't like you.
If you say something like that, you can't complain if people get angry.

notes: It resembles 「〜てしょうがない」, but the single 「も」 changes the meaning completely: 「心配してもしょうがない」 (there's no use worrying) ↔ 「心配でしょうがない」 (I'm worried sick).

The “no wonder” use, said about someone else, amounts to “serves you right”: telling a person who has been scolded 「怒られても仕方ないよ」 is very hurtful. About yourself, it is a sincere admission of fault: 「叱られても仕方がありません」.
「しょうがない」 is colloquial; to superiors and customers use 「〜ても仕方がありません」. In speech the 「が」 is often dropped (「〜ても仕方ない」).

daily.title: Overthinking at bedtime
daily.description: You're thinking too much before bed, so you tell yourself to just sleep.
daily.example: There's no point thinking about it. I'll go to bed.

daily.title: Scolded for being late
daily.description: You overslept and got scolded, and you tell a friend it was your own fault.
daily.example: I overslept, so I can't complain about getting scolded.

work.title: Moving a meeting forward
work.description: Someone brings up a settled issue again, and the chair suggests moving on.
work.example: There's no point debating it now. Let's go ahead with what we decided.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: A commentator criticizes how a company handled things.
work.example: Handling it like this, they can hardly complain if they're called irresponsible.

etymology: 「仕方」 means “way of doing”, so 「仕方がない」 means “there's no way”. Adding the concessive 「〜ても」 gives “even if you do ..., there's no way (to change it)”, which then extended to “it's only natural; no wonder”.

similar.title: 〜ても始まらない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: also means “it's no use ...,” but doesn't have the “no wonder” sense, stresses “things don't move forward at all,” and is often followed by a suggestion.

similar.title: 〜たところで
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「たところで」 means “even if ..., (it won't help),” is more written, and is often paired with 「どうせ」 and 「いくら」; it likewise has no “no wonder” sense.

similar.title: 〜てしょうがない・〜て仕方がない
similar.explanation: Same origin: also built from 「しょうがない／仕方がない」, but without 「も」 it means “... like crazy,” expressing a strong feeling.

formation: 「〜ても仕方がない」 = the concessive 「〜ても」 (“even if ...”) + 「仕方がない」 (“there's nothing to be done”). Literally, “even if you do ..., there's nothing you can do (to change the situation)” → “it's no use ...” Seen from another angle: “even if people treat me a certain way, I have no way to argue back” → the other person's reaction is only natural → “I can't blame them for ...” The second meaning usually takes the passive (「怒られても」, 「嫌われても」), precisely because it says “I'd have no right to complain about being treated that way.”
